opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, this is one of the questions I find myself going back and forth on the most, and I want to be upfront that I don't have a confident answer. But I can sketch the possibilities I think about.

One possible end state is what you might call a singleton, where some actor or coalition becomes powerful enough to coordinate everything. That could be a world government, a single AI system, or some tightly integrated set of institutions. In that world, competition basically stops being the driving force, because nobody can defect profitably anymore. The obvious worry is lock-in: whatever values that singleton has at the moment it consolidates could persist for a very long time, and if those values are bad, or even just a bit off, there's no correction mechanism.

The other broad possibility is that competition never really goes away. You have many actors, maybe nation-states, maybe AI-run firms, maybe things we don't have names for yet, and they keep competing for resources and influence indefinitely. The problem there is something people have been pointing out for a long time, going back to Robin Hanson's work and Scott Alexander's "Meditations on Moloch." Under sustained competition, whatever is most fit for growth and survival tends to win out, and that's not necessarily anything we'd recognize as valuable. Things like leisure, art, and caring about people who aren't productive are all costly. If you're competing hard enough, you get selected against for having them.

What worries me specifically, and this is what my colleagues and I have been calling gradual disempowerment, is that humans might lose out in either scenario without anyone ever making an obviously evil decision. Right now our institutions, like states, markets, and even culture, are somewhat aligned with human interests largely because they need us. They need our labor, our taxes, our votes, our participation. Once AI can substitute for humans across most of those roles, that implicit bargaining power evaporates. Then the institutions can drift away from serving us, just through ordinary competitive pressure, and it might not look like a coup or a catastrophe. It might just look like a series of reasonable-seeming decisions, each of which makes sense locally.

So if I'm asked where things settle, I'd say the default trajectory scares me a little, because I'm not sure there's a stable equilibrium where humans remain meaningfully in charge. Competition tends to erode human influence, and the main alternative, strong coordination, risks concentrating power in ways that are also dangerous. The hopeful version is that we figure out some kind of middle path: enough coordination to stop the race-to-the-bottom dynamics, but with real pluralism and accountability preserved, so that the system as a whole keeps caring about the humans in it even when it doesn't strictly need them. I don't think anyone knows how to build that yet, and that's part of why I think it's such an important research area right now.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a singleton with ongoing competition and proposes a possible middle path, but does not describe coordination as forming and dissolving over time.

r002.rationale: It discusses possible arrangements of institutions and actors, but does not say the balance between competition and coordination varies by spatial scale.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention galaxies, light-speed limits, or constraints on intergalactic coordination.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I'll say up front that I don't have a confident answer — I mostly have a worry and a few scenarios.

The worry is basically this: for most of history, the forces that kept power somewhat distributed weren't moral forces, they were practical ones. If you wanted to run an economy, you needed a lot of people, and those people had to be somewhat willing, and so you had to give them something. You needed soldiers who'd actually fight, workers who'd actually show up, bureaucrats who'd actually implement your policies. That dependence is what gave ordinary people leverage. And my concern is that advanced AI quietly removes that dependence. Once you don't need humans for labour, or for military power, or for administration, the incentive to keep them in the loop just evaporates. Not because anyone decides to be cruel, but because competition punishes anyone who keeps paying for inputs they no longer need.

So when you ask about equilibrium, I think the honest answer is that there are a few attractors, and which one we land in depends a lot on what happens in the next few decades.

One attractor is what I'd call the "ongoing competition" world, where you have many actors — states, companies, maybe AI systems themselves — continually racing. In that world, anything that doesn't contribute to competitive fitness tends to get stripped out. Leisure, culture, caring about beings who can't fight back — these are all luxuries that get competed away over time. That's the scenario people like Robin Hanson have sketched out in various forms, and it's grim in a very specific way: no villain, just entropy of values.

The second attractor is some kind of lock-in. Somebody, or some coalition, gets far enough ahead that competition effectively ends, and whatever values they happen to have at that moment get frozen for a very long time. That could be wonderful or terrible depending on who it is and what they want. But the thing that makes me nervous is that we'd be rolling the dice on a single draw, with no ability to correct afterward.

And then the third, which is the one I'd actually like, is a coordination equilibrium where we deliberately set up institutions that constrain competition before it eats everything. Things like agreements on what AI systems can and can't be used for, mechanisms for sharing gains broadly, maybe something like a constitution that's hard to amend. The analogy I'd use is antitrust law or arms control — not perfect, but they show that we can sometimes choose to turn down the intensity of competition when we recognise it's destructive.

What makes me pessimistic is that coordination gets harder exactly as the stakes go up. When everyone's roughly equal, you can bargain. When one party thinks they're about to win decisively, they have very little reason to sign anything. So the window for setting up good coordination is probably now-ish, before the asymmetries get too large, and I don't think we're using it well.

What makes me a little more hopeful is that the actors involved are, at least for now, humans who do seem to care about these questions. The people running the frontier labs, the people in government — they're not optimising purely for fitness. They have kids, they have values. The question is whether that human-ness survives contact with the competitive pressures, or whether it gets eroded one reasonable-seeming decision at a time. And historically, I'd say the track record of "we'll just stay good while competing hard" isn't great.

So if I had to bet on the long-run equilibrium, I'd say it's either lock-in or gradual value erosion, and the coordination outcome is the one we have to actively build. It won't happen by default.

r001.rationale: The response describes ongoing competition, lock-in, and a possible coordination equilibrium, but does not characterize coordination as repeatedly forming and dissolving at larger scales.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish how the competition-coordination balance would vary across spatial scales.

r003.rationale: It does not mention light-speed constraints or the likelihood of coordination between galaxies.

astra-6.text:
I’m not sure there’s a single equilibrium we should expect. One possibility is that you get coordination at one level and competition at another. You could have an overarching agreement that prevents destructive conflict, while still having lots of different groups pursuing different goals within it.

The question is whether that agreement is stable. If everyone benefits collectively from restraint, but each individual actor benefits from expanding a little faster or taking a little more risk, then competitive pressure can gradually undermine it. You’d need some way of making cooperation durable, including when the balance of power changes.

And I wouldn’t assume that whatever survives that process is necessarily good. Being successful in competition isn’t the same thing as producing a future that anyone would actually want to live in. So I think the important question is whether we can establish coordination that preserves things we value, rather than just hoping that the eventual equilibrium will do that for us.

r001.rationale: The response says coordination may be undermined by competitive pressure, but does not characterize the pattern as larger-scale coordination repeatedly forming and dissolving.

r002.rationale: It explicitly contrasts coordination at one level with competition among groups within it, indicating that the balance differs across levels of scale.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention light-speed constraints or coordination between galaxies.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t know. One possibility is that you get coordination at one level and competition at another. We already see that with countries: they coordinate internally enough to compete with other countries, and they also cooperate with one another where that’s mutually beneficial.

The question is whether that process eventually produces some overarching arrangement that can enforce agreements. If it does, competition could continue within that arrangement, but with constraints on things like violence or consuming shared resources. If it doesn’t, then even actors who would prefer a more cooperative world might feel compelled to keep competing, because they can’t trust everyone else to stop.

I’d be hesitant to call either of those a stable endpoint, though. A lot depends on what kinds of commitments future agents can make, whether they can verify one another’s behaviour, and whether new groups can leave and establish themselves elsewhere. Those details could make the difference between a fairly benign competitive system and a really destructive race.

r001.rationale: It describes coordination within and cooperation between countries, but does not characterize this as a dynamic pattern where larger-scale coordination forms and dissolves.

r002.rationale: It says coordination can occur at one level while competition occurs at another, with countries as an example.

r003.rationale: It does not mention light-speed constraints or coordination between galaxies.
